findings.harm: importing the package's published barrel performs synchronous disk I/O and can throw at module-evaluation time. Every consumer of @systemfsoftware/stryker-js-typescript-checker pays it, including a consumer that only wants the type surface; a missing or malformed schema/typescript-checker-options.json is an unrecoverable module-load crash with no typed error channel, so nothing downstream can catch or retry it.
findings.adjudication: read confirms readFileSync + JSON.parse + S.decodeUnknownSync at indentation zero on lines 14-21, outside any function body and unguarded by a main check (FP2 satisfied). This is the package's public barrel, so the blast radius is every consumer.

findings.harm: the engine's version/engines constants are produced by reading package.json off disk at import time, so importing any module that transitively reaches this file performs I/O and can throw before any error channel exists. The CLI's own engine guard (cli/src/main.ts:18) depends on it, so a packaging change that moves package.json breaks the binary at load rather than at a decode boundary.
findings.adjudication: read confirms fs.readFileSync at line 10 inside a module-scope const initializer at indentation zero, followed by S.decodeUnknownSync at line 15, both outside any function body.

findings.harm: a module-scope mutable cache is shared by every importer in the process and is never invalidated, so a second checker instance in the same process observes the first instance's TypeScript version. It also makes the module's behaviour order-dependent, which no test that imports it fresh can reproduce.
findings.adjudication: read confirms `let cachedTSVersion: string | undefined` at indentation zero on line 35, mutated by getTSVersion at line 37; shipped source, not a fixture.

findings.harm: the process exit classification is accumulated in a module-scope mutable Set, so two runs in one process share it and the second run's exit code is a function of the first. It is unreachable from a typed channel, so no caller can scope, reset, or inspect it.
findings.adjudication: read confirms `const pendingExitClasses: Set<ExitClass> = new Set()` at indentation zero on line 13, mutated by setPendingExitClass at line 15. Constructing an empty Set is inert (FP1), so this is graded as shared mutable module state (FP5), not as an import-time effect.

findings.harm: a third-party stateful client (diff-match-patch) is instantiated once at module scope and shared by every caller, so its tunable fields (Diff_Timeout and friends) are process-global. A caller that adjusts them changes every other caller's diff, and no test can isolate the instance.
findings.adjudication: read confirms `const diffMatchPatch = new DiffMatchPatch()` at indentation zero on line 26. Graded as a module-scope shared client (FP5), not counted in the composition-root total (FP1).

findings.harm: the published plugin protocol types every method as returning an eager Promise, so a plugin's work cannot be held, retried, timed out, or interrupted as a value: the engine must build ad-hoc timeout and kill machinery around it (worker-pool/kill.ts, tree-kill) instead of composing Effect combinators. Because it is the contract package, every plugin any adopter writes inherits the defect.
findings.adjudication: read confirms `init(): Promise<void>`, `check(mutants): Promise<Record<...>>`, `group?(): Promise<string[][]>` on the exported Checker interface — an eager async result on the published surface, which CONST-B2 names exactly.

findings.harm: the subsystem's object graph is assembled by a third-party DI container whose types reach the published .d.ts (commonTokens, tokens, Injector<...>, PluginContext, BaseContext), so every adopter writing a plugin must install typed-inject and every wiring decision is expressed in a vocabulary the repo does not own. Effect's own Layer/Context.Tag is already a dependency of this same package, so the container buys nothing the runtime does not already supply, while adding a mandatory transitive dependency to the whole plugin ecosystem.
findings.adjudication: read confirms typed-inject imported in 19 files and its token vocabulary used at 168 sites across 47 files, including re-exports from the contract package's published surface; 16 `static inject` declarations bind classes to the container.

findings.harm: the engine's concurrency core is expressed in rxjs (zip, mergeMap, takeUntil, ignoreElements, BehaviorSubject, ReplaySubject) while the process it runs in is an Effect program, so cancellation, backpressure and error propagation cross two unrelated schedulers. An interrupted Effect fiber does not interrupt an rxjs subscription, which is how a killed run leaves child processes alive.
findings.adjudication: read confirms rxjs imported in 5 files with 43 operator/subject uses, driving the worker pool that owns every child process; Effect's Stream.mapEffect (concurrency), Semaphore.withPermits, Effect.retry/timeout and Fiber.interruptAll are all present in the vendored repos/effect tree and cover the same semantics.

findings.harm: failures are raised as thrown Error subclasses and recovered with 88 try/catch blocks, so no caller can branch on a failure variant at the type level and the compiler cannot tell a caller it forgot a case. The subsystem already depends on effect, whose Schema.TaggedError gives each failure its own dispatchable variant; zero of them exist here, so every error path is untyped.
findings.adjudication: read confirms StrykerError extends Error and is thrown; the sweep counts 113 `throw new` sites in 53 files and 88 try/catch openings in 30 files, against 0 matches for Schema.TaggedError across the subsystem.

findings.harm: a mutator is a domain decision — AST node in, replacement set out — and this one decides through a six-arm if/else-if chain with nested ifs. Every arm is a path the mutator's own mutation score must cover, and because the branching is control flow rather than exhaustive dispatch over a closed type, adding an AST node kind compiles silently and produces no mutants for it.
findings.adjudication: read confirms the six-way if/else-if chain plus nested ifs in the mutate body; the same file is the slice's worst offender out of 16 mutators, none of which is constructed through Workflow.make.

findings.harm: process spawning and killing are done through execa, npm-run-path and tree-kill rather than @effect/platform's Command/CommandExecutor, so the engine's most dangerous I/O sits outside the runtime that owns interruption. A fiber interrupt cannot reach a process the platform layer never created, which is the mechanism behind orphaned child processes on a cancelled run; and three third-party packages are load-bearing on the kill path.
findings.adjudication: read confirms tree-kill wrapped in a hand-rolled Promise.withResolvers to SIGKILL a process tree, alongside 4 direct node:child_process imports and 4 direct node:fs imports elsewhere in the same package.

findings.harm: the IPC boundary is a class holding nine mutable fields, including a correlation-id Map of in-flight calls and a fatalError latch. The invariants tying those fields together are enforced by nothing, so a partially failed dispose leaves a proxy that is neither alive nor dead; and because the object is reached through the DI container rather than a Layer, its lifetime is not scoped to anything the runtime can finalize.
findings.adjudication: read confirms the class and its mutable field set; the sweep counts 110 class declarations in 92 files and 333 assignment-initialised member lines in 106 files across the subsystem, none of them a Layer-provided Effect service.

findings.harm: the stryker binary is one process and is entitled to exactly one interpretation edge (cli/src/main.ts:48, NodeRuntime.runMain). Two further Effect.runSync sites sit inside an adapter, so part of the program is interpreted from within the program: work started there is outside the root's fiber tree, so it is not interrupted when the run is cancelled and its failures cannot reach the root's exit-code teardown.
findings.adjudication: read confirms NodeRuntime.runMain at cli/src/main.ts:48 as the declared root, and two Effect.runSync sites at RunEventStreamAdapter.ts:71 and :74 (line 65 is the doc comment naming them); the worker process's own root (child-process-proxy-worker-main.ts:12) is legitimate and counted separately under the multi-process rule.

findings.locator: grep '\bWorkflow\.make\(' over packages/testing/mutation/stryker-js (1 match, 1 file) vs the same locator over packages/**/*.ts (control: 122 matches, 19 files)
findings.harm: the repo's own law makes Workflow.make the boundary that constructs a pure decision and Cell.read/decode/decide/encode/write the shape of a shell, and the mutation gate the subsystem itself ships keys its population on that boundary. Across 27,500 lines there is exactly one Workflow.make call and zero phase chains, so the subsystem's decisions sit where its own mutation instrument cannot see them: a perfect score would certify nothing. RunResultHelpers is the sharpest instance — a domain decision (toMutantRunResult, determineHitLimitReached) authored as if/switch/ternary inside the contract package, which is excluded from mutation by construction.
findings.adjudication: read confirms the decision logic in RunResultHelpers.ts within plugin-api, and the sweep confirms 1 Workflow.make site (cli/src/Survivors.workflow.ts:442), 0 Cell phase-chain sites and 0 Schema.TaggedError sites subsystem-wide, against 122 Workflow.make matches in 19 files and 68 phase-chain matches elsewhere in packages/.

findings.harm: @systemfsoftware/stryker-js-util is a published package whose base segment answers 'of what?' with nothing, so no adopter can predict what installing it gives them and no author can decide whether a new helper belongs in it. That is not cosmetic: the name is why eight unrelated capabilities accumulated in one unit, and why three of its modules are dead without anyone noticing.
findings.adjudication: read confirms the published name @systemfsoftware/stryker-js-util; per package-naming.md the qualifier stryker-js is the product's own family name and narrows nothing, so the junk word is bare. Directory violations instrumenter/src/util/ (6 files, `git ls-files` verified) and plugin-api/src/core/ (12 files, `git ls-files` verified) carry the same finding; testResources fixture paths and the qualified names reporter-util.ts, string-utils.ts and base-preset.ts are DISMISSED as passing the 'of what?' test or out of shipped scope.

findings.harm: mutation-run holds at least nine capabilities behind one manifest — config resolution, plugin loading, project/file discovery, sandbox filesystem staging, child-process pooling, test-runner orchestration, checker orchestration, incremental diffing, logging transport and reporter fan-out. One change touches several, no consumer can bind one without the rest, and the unit cannot be reasoned about or replaced piecewise. util holds eight unrelated ones, mutation-report four, plugin-api three.
findings.adjudication: read confirms the subdirectory split (config 18, worker-pool 17, sandbox 11, logging 11, test-runner 10, checker 7, run-stages 6, project 6, plugins 5, mutants 5, reporting 4 files) with no shared decision boundary between them; each subtree has its own third-party dependency set and its own class hierarchy.

findings.harm: the reporter package imports runtime values from the engine it reports on (injectionTokens, isActionableStatus, and the Timer class), so the arrow points from the presentation edge into the engine. A reporter cannot be published, versioned or tested without the whole engine, and the engine's internals become the reporter's compile-time surface — which is why the subsystem's own AGENTS.md has to instruct agents to rebuild the engine before testing a reporter change.
findings.adjudication: read confirms three runtime-value imports at progress-stream-reporter.ts:6-8 and the Timer class import at progress-keeper.ts:15 — values, not types-only, so the edge survives type erasure and is a real runtime dependency.

findings.harm: three modules are exported from a published package and imported by nothing: childProcessAsPromised (which also drags node:child_process onto the surface), platform.caseSensitiveFs and escapeRegExpLiteral. Dead exported code is worse than dead private code, because an adopter may bind it and the repo has no test, no owner and no reason to keep it correct.
findings.adjudication: the search returns only the definition sites and the barrel re-export at util/src/index.ts:1 — no consumer anywhere in packages/, omp/, scripts/ or agent-plugins/. A fourth exported symbol, the `DeepPartial` type in deep-merge.ts, has the same zero-consumer status and is covered by this finding. Absence is the citation.

findings.locator: grep '@ts-(expect-error|ignore|nocheck)' over the subsystem, adjudicated: 1 real suppression, the remaining textual hits are the `@ts-nocheck` string literals that instrumenter/src/disable-type-checks.ts INSERTS into sandboxed files plus JSON-schema prose
findings.harm: a type error at the Vitest option boundary is silenced rather than modelled, so the runner passes both the removed `threads` option and its replacement `pool: 'threads'`. When Vitest removes the compatibility path the suppression keeps compiling and the option is silently ignored, changing the isolation model of every mutant run without a diagnostic.
findings.adjudication: read confirms `// @ts-expect-error threads got renamed to "pool: threads" in vitest 1.0.0` immediately above `threads: true` at line 134, with `pool: 'threads'` on the next line — both options are passed. vitest-runner/AGENTS.md:5 records the suppression as deliberately inherited, which REF4 refuses as prior approval.

findings.locator: grep '(eslint|oxlint)-disable' over the subsystem (20 matches, 11 files; 19 of them `eslint-disable-next-line` in 10 files under src/) cross-checked against `git ls-files | grep -i eslint | grep -v '^repos/'` -> 0 non-vendored eslint config files, and the per-package devDependency scan showing oxlint in all 8 manifests and eslint in none
findings.harm: twenty `eslint-disable` comments across eleven files suppress a linter this repo does not run, so each one is a standing instruction about a rule that cannot fire. They read as deliberate exemptions and will be preserved by the next author on that belief, while the oxlint rule that actually governs the line is unsuppressed and unexamined — the reader is misinformed in both directions.
findings.adjudication: the search returns 0 non-vendored eslint configs and 0 eslint devDependencies against oxlint in all 8 manifests, so every one of the 20 comments is inert. Adjudicated under deletability rather than as a suppression finding: it suppresses nothing, so REF4's 'adjudicate the code beneath it' resolves to 'the code beneath it is already governed by oxlint'.

findings.locator: per-package devDependency scan for @systemfsoftware/oxlint-plugin-{cell-vocabulary,effect-entrypoint,test-placement} across the 8 manifests: present in cli only, absent in 7
findings.harm: the three oxlint plugins that make the target idiom executable — cell-vocabulary (phase-body purity), effect-entrypoint (interpretation edges), test-placement (test tiers) — are registered by the cli package alone. In the other seven packages the law is present in no window and gates no command, so it has zero reach: a rewrite can regress the day after it lands and every check still exits 0. Any plan that rewrites those packages without registering the plugins ships an unmeasured architecture.
findings.adjudication: the scan confirms cli declares all three plugins and instrumenter, mutation-report, mutation-run, plugin-api, typescript-checker, util and vitest-runner declare only @systemfsoftware/oxlint-config and oxlint. Recorded as SURVIVED because the missing enrolment is itself the defect the audit exists to surface, not a preference.
